edits.old:

edits.new:
$U(t,x)+c(t)$ with a differentiable function $c$ of $t$ alone whenever
the declared $C^{2}$ regularity is retained. More generally, for each connected
component $C$ of $Q$ (a maximal connected subset), two $C^{2}$ potentials
for the same force differ by an independently chosen $C^{2}$ function
$c_C(t)$ on $I_0\times C$. A single time function suffices when $Q$ is

edits.reason: Full componentwise converse with local constancy argument
edits.old:
**(c) Normalization of the potential.** Let $c:I_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be
differentiable and let $\tilde U:=U+c(t)$. Since $\nabla_{x_{i}}\tilde
U=\nabla_{x_{i}}U$, the function $\tilde U$ presents the same potential part
$-∇_{x_{i}}\tilde U=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ with the same residual forces $d_{i}$;
conversely every $C^{2}$ potential presenting the same potential part differs
from $U$ by a function of $t$ alone, because the gradient in $x$ vanishes
exactly for such functions. Hence the potential of a presentation is
determined only up to an additive differentiable function $c(t)$ of the time
coordinate. The representative is part of the model's declaration, and every
energy statement of the framework names the representative it uses; the
derivative of $c$ enters the balance of the energy-balance item of this page.
edits.new:
**(c) Normalization of the potential.** Let $c:I_0\to\mathbb R$ be
differentiable and put $\widetilde U:=U+c(t)$, retaining $C^2$ regularity
when a potential presentation of the standing class is required. The spatial
gradient is unchanged, so this presents the same potential part with the same
residual forces. The full converse is componentwise: if $\widetilde U$ and
$U$ are $C^2$ and have the same spatial gradient, then on each connected
component $C$ of the open set $Q$ there is a $C^2$ function
$c_C:I_0\to\mathbb R$ with
$$\widetilde U(t,x)-U(t,x)=c_C(t)\qquad(x\in C).$$
Here a connected component is a maximal connected subset of $Q$. For fixed
$t$, the difference is constant on every ball contained in $Q$: along any
segment in the ball its derivative is the vanishing spatial gradient paired
with the segment direction. The difference is consequently locally constant,
and on a connected component it is constant, since a value's level set and
its complement are both relatively open. Evaluating at any fixed point of
$C$ gives the $C^2$ regularity of $c_C$. Conversely, independent such functions
on the components give a $C^2$ potential with unchanged spatial gradient;
components of an open Euclidean set are open, because each sufficiently small
ball about one of their points is connected and lies in that component.
A single $c(t)$ describes every ambiguity precisely when the component
functions agree, in particular when $Q$ is connected. No agreement follows
from openness alone: on two disjoint balls the potentials $0$ and the function
equal to $0$ on one ball and $1$ on the other have the same force. Every
continuous motion on an interval remains in one component, so its energy
shifts by that component's $c_C(t)$ and its energy rate by $c_C'(t)$.
The representative is part of the model's declaration, and every energy
statement names it.

edits.old:
- **The shape of the hypothesis.** Hypothesis (i) is the invariance of the
  potential under the simultaneous translation of all labels by a common
  vector, and it is strictly stronger than the statement that each
  $\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is annihilated by $a$ at one point; hypothesis (ii) makes
  the invariance reading explicit, the equivalence being valid on the possibly
  nonconvex open set $Q$ because the translation line meets $Q$ in an open
  interval on which the derivative argument is applied. For a pair-presented
  model with two-body potentials the condition holds identically, which is the
  familiar conservation of total momentum; the Noether route here uses the
  potential presentation and $d\equiv0$, while the balance theorem
  [[pthm-cm03-momentum-balance]] obtains its conservation statement from the
  antisymmetric pair presentation, and neither route implies the other's
  hypotheses.
edits.new:
- **The shape of the hypothesis.** Condition (i) is infinitesimal
  translation invariance and needs no convexity or connectedness of $Q$.
  It is equivalent to finite invariance along every segment contained in $Q$.
  Comparing admissible endpoints across an excluded segment additionally
  requires the component constants of clause 1 to agree. This qualification
  cannot be omitted: on two disjoint balls with centres on the translation
  axis, a potential equal to $0$ on one and $1$ on the other has zero
  directional derivative everywhere but fails endpoint invariance.
  The momentum conservation and sharpness clauses retain their full scope
  under the differential hypothesis on arbitrary open $Q$. For a
  pair-presented translation-invariant potential that hypothesis holds
  identically; the Noether route uses the potential presentation and
  $d\equiv0$, while [[pthm-cm03-momentum-balance]] uses antisymmetric pair
  forces, and neither route implies the other's hypotheses.

edits.old:
1. **(two forms of the hypothesis).** The following are equivalent:
   (i) $\sum_{i=1}^{N}a\cdot\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)=0$ for every
   $(t,x)\in I_{0}\times Q$; (ii) $U(t,x+s\xi^{a})=U(t,x)$ for every
   $(t,x)\in I_{0}\times Q$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$ with $x+s\xi^{a}\in Q$.
edits.new:
1. **(infinitesimal and finite invariance).** The following are equivalent:
   (i) $\sum_{i=1}^N a\cdot\nabla_{x_i}U(t,x)=0$ for every
   $(t,x)\in I_0\times Q$; (ii) $U(t,x+s\xi^a)=U(t,x)$ whenever
   the whole segment $\{x+r\xi^a:r\text{ between }0\text{ and }s\}$
   lies in $Q$. More generally, for fixed $(t,x)$ put
   $J_x:=\{s\in\mathbb R:x+s\xi^a\in Q\}$, an open set containing $0$.
   Its interval components are its maximal open intervals. Under (i),
   $s\mapsto U(t,x+s\xi^a)$ is constant on each interval component.
   Invariance for every $s\in J_x$, including components separated by an
   excluded segment, holds if and only if all these component constants
   equal $U(t,x)$. This agreement is automatic when $J_x$ is connected,
   in particular when the whole translation line lies in $Q$.

edits.old: 1.1 Clause 1, (i) implies (ii): fix $(t,x)\in I_{0}\times Q$ and let $J_{x}:=\{s\in\mathbb R:x+s\xi^{a}\in Q\}$, an open interval containing $0$ because $Q$ is open and $s\mapsto x+s\xi^{a}$ is continuous; the function $f(s):=U(t,x+s\xi^{a})$ is $C^{1}$ on $J_{x}$ with $f'(s)=\sum_{i}a\cdot\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x+s\xi^{a})$ by the chain rule, which vanishes on $J_{x}$ under hypothesis (i), so $f$ is constant on $J_{x}$ by [F6]; hence $U(t,x+s\xi^{a})=U(t,x)$ for every $s\in J_{x}$, which is (ii). [F6, given, algebra]
edits.new: 1.1 Clause 1, (i) implies (ii): for fixed $(t,x)$ the set $J_x$ is open by continuity of $s\mapsto x+s\xi^a$, but can have several interval components. On each such interval $f(s):=U(t,x+s\xi^a)$ is $C^1$ with derivative $\sum_i a\cdot\nabla_{x_i}U(t,x+s\xi^a)=0$ under (i), hence is constant by [F6]. If the entire segment between $0$ and $s$ is admissible, both parameters lie in the same interval component, so $f(s)=f(0)$, proving (ii). The same calculation proves constancy on every component; equality at every admissible endpoint holds exactly when all component constants equal $f(0)$, and is automatic for connected $J_x$. [F6, given, algebra]

## Remarks

- **Separated arcs.** On two disjoint balls centred at opposite points of
  a circle about the axis, the potential equal to $0$ on one ball and $1$
  on the other has zero rotational derivative everywhere, but a rotation
  between the two centres changes its value. Differential conservation
  holds on arbitrary open $Q$; comparing separated arcs requires the
  compatibility in clause 1.

1. **(two forms of the hypothesis).** The following are equivalent:
   (i) $\sum_{i}\bigl\langle a\times x_{i},\,\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)\bigr\rangle=0$
   for every $(t,x)\in I_{0}\times Q$; (ii) $U(t,R_{a}(s)x)=U(t,x)$ for every
   $(t,x)\in I_{0}\times Q$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$ with
   $R_{a}(s)x\in Q$.
edits.new:
1. **(infinitesimal and finite invariance).** The following are equivalent:
   (i) $\sum_i\langle a\times x_i,\nabla_{x_i}U(t,x)\rangle=0$
   for every $(t,x)\in I_0\times Q$; (ii) $U(t,R_a(s)x)=U(t,x)$
   whenever $\{R_a(r)x:r\text{ between }0\text{ and }s\}$ lies in $Q$.
   More generally put $D_x:=\{s\in\mathbb R:R_a(s)x\in Q\}$, an open set
   containing $0$, with interval components its maximal open intervals.
   Under (i), $s\mapsto U(t,R_a(s)x)$ is constant on each interval
   component. Invariance for every $s\in D_x$, including components
   separated by an excluded arc, holds if and only if all these constants
   equal $U(t,x)$. This agreement is automatic if $D_x$ is connected,
   in particular if the whole rotation orbit is contained in $Q$.

4. **(boosted motions).** Under the hypotheses of clause 2, let $x:J\to Q$ be
   a motion and let $s\in\mathbb R$ be such that $x(t)+s\,t\,\xi^{a}_1\in Q$
   for every $t\in J$, where $\xi^{a}_1=(a,\dots,a)$; then

edits.new:
4. **(boosted motions).** Under the hypotheses of clause 2, let $x:J\to Q$
   be a motion and $s\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $x(t)+st\xi^a_1\in Q$ for every
   $t\in J$, where $\xi^a_1=(a,\dots,a)$. Then
   $\widetilde x(t):=x(t)+st\xi^a_1$ is a motion if and only if
   $\nabla_xU(t,\widetilde x(t))=\nabla_xU(t,x(t))$ for every $t\in J$.
   This equality, and hence the boosted-motion conclusion, follows if
   each segment between $x(t)$ and $\widetilde x(t)$ is contained in $Q$,
   or if the all-admissible-endpoint finite invariance criterion of
   [[pthm-cm08-translation]] clause 1 holds.

abla_xU(t,\widetilde x)$ is therefore equivalent to $
abla_xU(t,\widetilde x)=
abla_xU(t,x)$, since $x$ is a motion. If every joining segment lies in $Q$, the derivative along that segment of $
abla_xU$ is $
abla_x(\xi^a_1\cdot
abla_xU)=0$ by the differential hypothesis and [F6], giving the equality.
